hook: When flat chunks stop answering — **graphs, agents, multi-hop, and security**. The frontier toolkit for questions that span documents and permissions.

scenes.title: Some questions need a **map**, not a pile of chunks
scenes.narration: Flat retrieval has a structural blind spot: it finds chunks similar to the query but can't see RELATIONSHIPS — how entities connect across a whole corpus. 'Which suppliers depend on the same subcomponent as our top product?' is a graph question. GraphRAG's recipe: during ingest, extract entities and relationships from every chunk — product, supplier, component, depends-on — and build a knowledge graph alongside the vector index. At query time, answer in two modes: local questions still go to plain vector search, but global or cross-document questions traverse the graph — or synthesize over graph-derived community summaries. You pay extraction cost and graph upkeep for questions flat RAG structurally cannot answer.

items.s: Entities + relations per chunk → graph beside the vector index · extraction LLM pass
"What's our refund window?" — flat retrieval still wins on speed & simplicity
Cross-doc relationships, dependencies, "who connects to whom" → traversal + community summaries

scenes.narration: The honest decision framework. GraphRAG is not an upgrade you apply everywhere — it's a different index answering a different question class. If your users ask lookup and summarization questions, vectors are simpler, cheaper and better. If they ask relationship and synthesis questions across the corpus — dependency analysis, influence mapping, 'what connects these two projects' — a graph earns its complexity. Start flat; add the graph when question analysis shows the relationship class appearing in your logs. Extraction quality gates everything: a noisy entity extractor builds a noisy graph, and graph errors are harder to spot than bad chunks.

scenes.title: Stop fetching on every question. **Let the model decide.**
scenes.sub: Retrieval as a tool, invoked when needed
scenes.narration: Classic RAG retrieves blindly: every question triggers the same pipeline, whether it needs documents or not. 'What's 2 + 2' doesn't need a corpus. Agentic RAG hands the loop to an agent: the LLM sees the question and a retrieval TOOL, plans — do I even need to search? what should I search for? — calls retrieval, reads the result, and decides whether to search again, answer, or ask the user for clarification. Trade-offs, plainly: you get judgment — no wasted retrievals, adaptive multi-step research — but you add latency, non-determinism and a harder eval surface, because each run takes a different path. Use it when questions genuinely vary in retrieval need; keep classic RAG where every question is a document question.

messages.text: Compare our SLA to the vendor's and flag gaps.
I'll need both documents. Searching for our SLA… found §3. Now the vendor agreement… found their §9. Comparing response-time clauses…
Gap found: we commit to 4h response, the vendor to 24h — and their penalty clause only triggers after 3 breaches.

scenes.narration: Watch the agent's reasoning trace: it DECIDED to retrieve twice, once per document, and each search was informed by the previous result — the second query targeted the vendor's section nine specifically. Classic RAG would have embedded the whole comparison question once, retrieved a blurry average of both documents, and summarized vaguely. The agent version costs two retrieval rounds and an orchestration loop, and buys a specific, verifiable answer. That's the agentic trade in one scene: spend control flow to get precision. Frameworks like LangGraph model this loop explicitly — nodes for retrieve, grade, rewrite, answer — which you'll meet again in the Agentic stages.

scenes.title: Chained questions need **chained retrieval**
scenes.narration: 'How does the team's headcount compare to the project budget?' requires two facts from two places, THEN a comparison. Single-shot retrieval fetches chunks about headcount OR budget — rarely both. Multi-hop pipelines decompose: an LLM splits the compound question into sub-questions, retrieves for each independently, then synthesizes the combined answer. It's the agentic pattern with a fixed plan instead of a free plan — cheaper and more evaluable, less flexible. The debug insight: evaluate each hop separately. If sub-question two retrieves garbage, the final synthesis inherits it — and the failure signature in logs is a good first hop followed by an empty second.

layers.s: Each sub-question → its own hybrid + rerank pass
All hop results + original question → one cited answer

scenes.narration: Three hops, three failure surfaces — which is why multi-hop demands per-hop evaluation. Decompose can mangle the question: 'compare X to Y' split into sub-questions that each lose the comparison intent. Retrieval per hop inherits everything from GA-15 — golden sets per sub-question. Synthesis can drop a hop's evidence or compare unequal units — the check is citations: a multi-hop answer should cite EVERY hop's sources, and a citation count lower than the hop count is a red flag you can assert on programmatically. Start with decomposition for predictable compound questions; graduate to full agentic control when the question shapes stop fitting a fixed template.

scenes.title: The two boring systems that **make RAG shippable**
scenes.narration: Security first: retrieval must respect access control. The pattern: attach ACL metadata to every chunk at ingest — GA-14's metadata lesson — and filter at query time by the ASKING USER's permissions, inside the retrieval call, never after. Post-filtering leaks: the LLM can see chunks it shouldn't, even if the UI hides them. This is non-negotiable in multi-tenant and HR/legal corpora. Then caching: repeated and similar questions dominate real traffic. A semantic cache stores question-embedding → answer pairs; a new question within a similarity threshold of a cached one gets the cached answer instantly — near-zero cost, near-zero latency. Cache below a similarity threshold only; near-duplicates at 0.97, not paraphrases at 0.85, or wrong answers get served fast.

items.s: Chunk carries permissions · query filters by asking user · NEVER post-filter after the LLM
Similar questions → cached answer · high threshold (≥0.97) · huge cost/latency win on repetitive traffic
Cache key includes user/tenant — never serve one user's cached answer to another

scenes.narration: Details that bite. ACL filtering belongs in the where-clause of the vector search — GA-09 taught you filtered retrieval; this is its production purpose. Post-filtering after generation is not security, it's hope. On caching, the threshold is the whole game: tune it on your own traffic, log cache hits, and include tenant and permission set in the cache key — a shared cache across users is a data-leak machine wearing a performance costume. These two systems are 'boring' the way brakes are boring: nobody demos them, and nothing ships safely without them. Stage 4 closes here — RAG from bytes to production.

scenes.title: Embeddings → vectors → retrieval → grounded answers. Done.
scenes.next: Reel 34 · Stage 5: App Building — turning pipelines into products

recap: GraphRAG: entity/relation extraction at ingest; graph traversal for cross-document relationship questions, vectors for local ones
Agentic RAG = retrieval as a tool under model control (judgment for latency/cost); multi-hop = fixed decompose-retrieve-synthesize for compound questions
Ship-ready = ACL filters inside retrieval (never post-filter) + semantic cache with high similarity threshold and tenant-scoped keys

quiz.q: When is GraphRAG worth its added complexity?
opts: When questions are relationship/global across the corpus (dependencies, influences) that flat chunk similarity structurally can't answer
quiz.why: Graphs index relationships, not text; local lookup and summarization questions remain simpler and better on plain vectors.

quiz.q: Why must access-control filtering happen inside the retrieval query rather than after generation?
opts: Post-filtering still shows forbidden chunks to the LLM — the model can leak them even if the UI hides them
quiz.why: Security lives at the retrieval boundary: chunks the user may not see must never enter the model's context at all.

quiz.q: What failure does per-hop evaluation in multi-hop RAG catch?
opts: A later sub-question retrieving garbage that the final synthesis silently inherits — visible as good first hop, empty second
quiz.why: Compound answers are only as good as the weakest hop; evaluating only the final answer hides which hop broke.

code.title: Advanced RAG guardrails: ACL filter + semantic cache + decomposition
annot: The where-clause is the security boundary — post-filtering is not security, it's hope
Cache key carries tenant AND uses a high threshold; a loose shared cache leaks data at high speed
Multi-hop keeps each hop independently retrievable — you can unit-test hop 2 without running hop 1

notes:
# Advanced RAG

## GraphRAG
- Ingest: LLM-extract entities + relations → knowledge graph beside vector index.
- Local questions → vectors; global/relationship questions → graph traversal / community summaries.
- Start flat; add graph when logs show relationship-class questions.

## Agentic RAG
- Retrieval becomes a TOOL the agent invokes: decide → search → read → re-search/answer/clarify.
- Wins: judgment, no wasted retrievals, adaptive depth.
- Costs: latency, non-determinism, harder eval. Fixed decomposition (multi-hop) is the middle ground.

## Multi-hop
- Decompose → retrieve per sub-question → synthesize.
- Evaluate EACH hop; answer must cite every hop's sources (citation count ≥ hop count).

## Security & caching
- ACL: chunk-level metadata, filtered in the retrieval query by asking user. Never post-filter.
- Semantic cache: q-embedding → answer, threshold ≥ ~0.97, key includes tenant.
- Stage 4 complete: ingest → chunk → embed → retrieve → generate → ship.
